title: Ring buffers and object pools
sub: head, count and a tail by modulo; a mask for a 2ᵏ capacity and frame history; pools, ObjectPool<T> and the double Release
cards/0/title: The problem, and where the ring lives in a game
cards/0/body:
Design Circular Queue (LeetCode #622). A FIFO queue on k fixed slots: EnQueue(v) and DeQueue() return false when they cannot work (full / empty); Front() and Rear() return the first and the last element or −1; plus IsEmpty() and IsFull(). Everything is O(1); k ≤ 1000, up to 3000 calls.

Signals of a ring buffer: a fixed capacity, “the oldest leaves first”, “the last N”, and no allocations after startup. In games the ring is everywhere: an input buffer (presses from the last few frames — for combos and for a jump pressed just before landing), the state history for rollback in a networked game, a replay of the last few seconds, a log of recent messages, the average FPS over the last frames.

.NET's Queue<T> is a ring inside too (collections unit), but when it fills up it doubles its array. Here growth is not allowed: full means a refusal, or, for a history, overwriting the oldest entry.
cards/0/code:
var q = new MyCircularQueue(3);
q.EnQueue(1); q.EnQueue(2); q.EnQueue(3);   // true, true, true
q.EnQueue(4);   // false: there are only 3 slots
q.Rear();       // 3
q.DeQueue();    // true: 1 is gone
q.EnQueue(4);   // true: 4 takes the freed slot 0
q.Rear();       // 4
cards/1/title: Empty or full: head == tail in both cases
cards/1/body:
The obvious state is two indices: head (where you take from) and tail (where the next one goes), both moving in a circle: (i + 1) % k. EnQueue writes to a[tail] and advances tail, DeQueue advances head. Nothing is shifted — everything is O(1).

The trap: in an empty queue head == tail, and in a full one too — the tail went all the way round and caught up with the head. Two indices cannot tell these states apart. Three ways out:

1. Keep a counter count: empty at 0, full at k.
2. Keep one slot always empty: full when (tail + 1) % k == head. The array then has k + 1 slots.
3. Indices that never wrap: head and tail only grow, the slot is i % k, the size is tail − head.

The tape's solution takes the first path and goes further: it stores head and count and computes the tail. One variable fewer means one fewer way to get out of sync.
cards/2/q: A queue on an array of 4 slots, only head and tail, no counter. 4 EnQueues in a row. What are head and tail?
cards/2/options/0: head = 0, tail = 0 — the same as an empty queue
cards/2/explain: tail advances four times by (tail + 1) % 4: 1, 2, 3 and back to 0. head did not move. The result is head == tail — exactly what an empty queue looks like. That is why you need count or one always-empty slot.
cards/2/wrong/1: Index 4 is outside an array of 4 slots: % 4 wraps it to 0.
cards/2/wrong/2: 3 is the slot of the last element. tail points to the next free slot, and after 3 the circle goes to 0.
cards/2/wrong/3: EnQueue advances tail, not head: the head moves only on DeQueue.
cards/3/title: head, count and a tail by modulo
cards/3/body:
The state is an array a of k slots, head and count. The tail — the next free slot — is (head + count) % k: past the end of the array the queue continues from slot 0. The last element is a[(head + count − 1) % k].

EnQueue: full (count == k) — false, nothing is overwritten; otherwise write to the tail and count++. DeQueue: empty — false; otherwise head = (head + 1) % k and count−−. The value stays in the array but is no longer part of the queue — no need to erase it. For a reference type T, clear the slot: otherwise the array keeps the object alive for the GC.

Invariant: the queue's elements are exactly count slots starting at head, going round. All operations are O(1), memory is k slots allocated once in the constructor.
cards/4/q: k = 5, head = 3, count = 4. Which slot does EnQueue write the next value to, and which slot holds Rear right now?
cards/4/options/0: Writes to 2, Rear is in slot 1
cards/4/options/1: Writes to 7, Rear is in slot 6
cards/4/options/2: Writes to 2, Rear is in slot 2
cards/4/options/3: Nowhere: the queue is full, EnQueue returns false
cards/4/explain: The tail is (3 + 4) % 5 = 2. The last element is (3 + 4 − 1) % 5 = 1. The queue occupies slots 3, 4, 0, 1 — four out of five, so there is room.
cards/4/wrong/1: 7 and 6 are indices without % 5: outside an array of 5 slots.
cards/4/wrong/2: Slot 2 is the tail, the next free one. The last element sits right before it — in slot 1.
cards/4/wrong/3: Full means count == k, and here count = 4 < 5.
cards/5/explain: Refuse when everything is taken: count == a.Length. The tail, the new head and Rear all go by modulo: without %, the indices leave the array as soon as the queue goes round. Rear is the slot before the tail.
cards/6/task: Walk the trace: k = 4. First the queue drifts away from the start of the array, then the tail and the head go round. The rig will ask twice what the code does.
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Nothing: the queue is full, false
cards/6/goal/asks/0/q: head = 2, count = 2, k = 4. Where does enQueue(5) write the value?
cards/6/goal/asks/0/explain: (2 + 2) % 4 = 0: the tail went past the end of the array and wrapped to slot 0. It is free — 1 was taken out of it long ago. The queue is full only when count == k, and count = 2.
cards/6/goal/asks/1/q: The queue is full: head = 2, count = 4. What does Rear() return?
cards/6/goal/asks/1/explain: The last element is in slot (2 + 4 − 1) % 4 = 1, which holds 6. a[2] holds 3 — that is the head, Front returns it. Without %, the index would be 5 — outside the array.
cards/7/q: k = 3: EnQueue(1), EnQueue(2), EnQueue(3), DeQueue(), EnQueue(4), Rear() — and Rear throws an IndexOutOfRangeException. Tap the buggy line.
cards/7/explain: After DeQueue head = 1, and EnQueue(4) went into slot 0 — the queue wrapped around. Rear computes 1 + 3 − 1 = 3 without % and runs off an array of 3 slots. It needs a[(head + count - 1) % a.Length] — the same formula as the tail, one slot earlier.
cards/8/title: A 2ᵏ capacity and a mask. History with overwrite
cards/8/body:
The mask. If the capacity is a power of two, i % cap for a non-negative i equals i & (cap − 1): the remainder of division by 2ᵏ is just the low k bits. Division is one of the slowest integer operations on a CPU, AND is one of the fastest, and an input buffer or a history computes an index on every write and every read.

With a mask, indices need not wrap at all: the write counter only grows, and the slot is tail & mask. An unsigned uint at 60 writes per second overflows after more than two years of non-stop play — and even then the index stays right: 2³² is divisible by any 2ᵏ capacity.

History with overwrite. An input buffer, a frame history or a replay do not want a refusal: full means the oldest entry is overwritten. Push writes to tail & mask and increments tail; the last cap entries are kept. “The i-th from the end” is buf[(tail − 1 − i) & mask]: “what was pressed 3 frames ago” is a single operation.

In Unity: 60 FPS × 10 seconds of replay = 600 frames → a capacity of 1024. The frame state is a struct in an array: zero allocations for the whole game. For Burst — a NativeArray<FrameState> with the same mask.
cards/9/q: A History<int> with 128 slots. Frame numbers 0, 1, …, 199 are written to it in order. What does Ago(0) return, and where is the oldest frame still stored?
cards/9/explain: tail = 200. The last 128 writes are kept — frames 72…199, the rest are overwritten. Frame f sits in slot f & 127: 72 & 127 = 72, and 199 is in slot 71. Ago(0) = buf[199 & 127] = 199. Slot 72 is the next one to be overwritten.
cards/9/wrong/1: Frame 0 was overwritten long ago: 200 writes into 128 slots — the first 72 are gone.
cards/9/wrong/2: Ago(0) is the latest write, 199. 127 is the number of the last slot, not the value in it.
cards/9/wrong/3: The slot is given by the write number, not by “where we started”: frame 72 was written to 72 & 127 = 72.
cards/10/title: Object pools and the double Release
cards/10/body:
A pool solves the same problem as the ring, but for objects: do not create and destroy them in a hot loop. Instantiate and Destroy are expensive, and Unity's managed garbage is collected by Boehm with no generations (C# and Unity unit).

How it works: a stack of free objects. Get pops one, or creates one if the stack is empty; Release resets the state and pushes it. A stack rather than a queue: the most recently returned object is most likely still in the CPU cache. Both operations are O(1).

UnityEngine.Pool.ObjectPool<T> (Unity 2021.1+) is a ready-made pool: delegates createFunc, actionOnGet, actionOnRelease, actionOnDestroy, and the sizes defaultCapacity and maxSize. If maxSize objects are already free, a returned object is destroyed through actionOnDestroy. Next to it are ListPool<T>, DictionaryPool, HashSetPool, LinkedPool<T>.

The double Release is the classic pool bug: a bullet went back to the pool on hit and once more on its timer. The object is on the stack twice, and the next two Gets hand the same object to two owners — two bullets on one GameObject. collectionCheck: true catches this with an exception, but only in the Editor; a player build has no check. A flag on the object itself is more reliable: Release checks and sets it, Get clears it. The same rule holds in .NET for ArrayPool<T>.Shared: an array is returned exactly once and never touched after Return.
cards/10/deep:
Warm-up. defaultCapacity is only the initial capacity of the internal stack: ObjectPool creates objects one at a time, on each Get from an empty pool. So that the first enemy wave does not cause a spike of Instantiate calls, warm the pool up during loading: take N objects and return them right away.

using. pool.Get(out var x) returns a PooledObject<T> that gives the object back in Dispose: using (ListPool<int>.Get(out var tmp)) { … } — a temporary list with no garbage and no forgotten Release. But do not keep the reference after the block: the list already belongs to its next owner.

ArrayPool<T>. Rent(n) returns an array at least n long, often longer — work with the first n elements, not with Length. The contents are not cleared: the array may hold someone else's data, and Return(arr, clearArray: true) wipes it on return. Shared is thread-safe; not returning an array is not a leak (the GC collects it), but it defeats the pool.

Threads and Jobs. ObjectPool<T> is not thread-safe — main thread only. Data in Burst does not need an object pool: the free slots of a NativeArray are chained into a free list of indices, as in the linked list unit.
cards/11/q: A bullet goes back to the pool on hit and on its timer; sometimes both happen in the same frame. What is true? Select all.
cards/11/options/0: A double Release puts the bullet into the pool twice, and two Gets hand out one object
cards/11/options/1: collectionCheck: true catches it in the Editor, but not in a player build
cards/11/options/2: A flag on the object that Release sets and Get clears catches it in a build too
cards/11/options/3: In a build, ObjectPool<T> skips a repeated Release by itself
cards/11/options/4: The garbage collector removes the extra copy from the pool's stack
cards/11/explain: A pool is a stack of references: one reference pushed twice comes out twice. The collectionCheck check runs only in the Editor, so in a build the bug is silent: two bullets share one object. A flag on the object costs one comparison and works everywhere. The GC has nothing to do with it: both references are live, there is no garbage.
cards/12/q: You are solving Design Circular Queue out loud. Put the steps in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: what to do when full — refuse or overwrite; what to return when empty
cards/12/items/1: Name the naive solution: a List<T> with RemoveAt(0) — O(n) on every DeQueue
cards/12/items/2: The idea: an array as a ring, head and count, tail = (head + count) % k
cards/12/items/3: Say why not two indices: both empty and full give head == tail
cards/12/items/4: Write the methods and walk an example where the tail goes round
cards/12/items/5: Complexity: O(1) per operation, k slots, no allocations after the constructor
cards/12/items/6: Improvements: a mask for a 2ᵏ capacity, overwrite for a frame history
cards/12/explain: “Refuse or overwrite” is the first question: these are two different structures. Explaining head == tail shows that you know the main trap, and a walk across the end of the array checks every %.
